lessons.transcript:
THE FIX FOR CRAVINGS — SESSION 2: PRACTICAL CRAVING BUSTERS — 20 MIN

— 0:00–0:30  HOOK —

Session One was the why. This session is the what: the busters, the tools I reach for when a craving is standing in the room, in the order I reach for them. Some of them take thirty seconds. One of them is a smoothie I'll make with you. And one of them is a date. Let's build your toolkit.

— 0:30–8:30  TOOLS —

Six tools, in roughly the order they work.

Tool one: the pause, from Session One. "There it is." Timer for ten minutes. Hands busy. I won't repeat the science; I'll just say that in my experience this one tool, used every time, does more than any food.

Tool two: sip. Warm and slow. The craving-buster tea from Module Two, cinnamon, ginger, vanilla, rooibos, or plain peppermint, chamomile, or hibiscus. Warm drinks occupy the hands and the mouth, the two things a craving wants, and warmth itself is soothing to the nervous system. On herbal remedies more broadly: I'm cautious, and I want you to be. Gentle teas are wonderful. Supplements sold as craving-cures, chromium, garcinia, "sugar-blocker" blends, have thin evidence and unknown interactions, and while you're trying to conceive they go to your doctor first, as does anything with licorice root or high-dose herbs. The only remedy in this course with strong evidence is a cup of something warm and the ten minutes it takes to drink it.

Tool three: move. The single best-evidenced craving buster outside of nutrition. Adrian Taylor's group at the University of Exeter found, in the journal Appetite, that a fifteen-minute brisk walk reduced cravings and snacking in regular chocolate eaters, and later work found the same for overweight adults and their sugary-snack cravings in a study in PLOS ONE. The mechanism is partly the blood sugar, partly the adrenaline burned off, and partly the scenery change. Your version doesn't have to be fifteen minutes: five minutes of stairs, a walk to the corner and back, thirty squats in the kitchen while the kettle boils. The craving wave lasts twenty minutes; a five-minute walk covers a quarter of it and comes back calmer.

Tool four: swap. The berries and walnuts, the dark chocolate and almonds, the yogurt bowl from Session One, the smoothie I'm about to make. Sweet with protein and fat, never sweet alone.

Tool five: connect. Text your person the word "craving." That's it. You don't need advice; you need to be seen for one second. Many people I've worked with have told me that a single reply, a heart, a "you've got this," was what got them through the wave. And for couples, that's the origin of the craving date, which I'll come to.

Tool six: sleep. Tonight's craving is fixed tomorrow morning by tonight's bedtime. If you've had three hard evenings in a row, the fix is not a better swap. It's an earlier night.

Match the tool to the root you mapped in Session One. Physical root, the three o'clock crash: swap and move. Environmental cue, the drawer, the show: rearrange, then sip. Emotional root, the hard evening: pause, connect, and the honest question about what you need. Sleep debt: the earlier night, full stop. The workbook has a matching table.

One more tool, which isn't in the six because it's less a tool than a rule: eat enough. A surprising number of evening cravings I've traced in my work turned out to be hunger, plain hunger, from a day of small, virtuous meals. Under-eating during the day is the most common physical root nobody suspects, and it's especially common in people who've been dieting for years. The fertility plate is not a small plate. Protein and fat at breakfast and lunch, enough that you're comfortably full for four hours. A body that's fed doesn't need to negotiate at nine.

— 8:30–15:30  DEMO: THE "FIX" SMOOTHIE —

Let me make the fix smoothie. This one is built specifically for the craving hour, so it's heavier on protein and fat than the breakfast smoothie from Module Two, and it tastes like a treat, which is the point.

One cup of plain whole-milk Greek yogurt or kefir; this is the protein, and if you don't do dairy, an unsweetened plant yogurt plus a scoop of unflavored protein. One tablespoon of unsweetened cocoa powder, because chocolate cravings are real and cocoa answers them without the sugar. One tablespoon of almond or peanut butter, for the fat that stops the rebound. Half a frozen banana, or a handful of frozen cherries if you want less sweetness. A handful of spinach; you won't taste it, and it's folate. A teaspoon of cinnamon, a pinch of salt, which makes the chocolate taste more chocolatey, and about half a cup of unsweetened milk of your choice. Ice if you like it thick.

Blend until smooth. Taste it. If it needs more sweetness, add a date, but taste first; the banana and the cocoa usually do it. This is dessert with about twenty grams of protein in it. It will hold you until morning, and it will not schedule a craving for tomorrow, which is the difference between this and the ice cream.

The two-minute version, for the night you can't face a blender: a small bowl of Greek yogurt, a spoon of cocoa stirred in, a spoon of nut butter on top, a few frozen cherries. Same nutrients, no machine, no washing up.

A story from my work, told the way I tell all of them, without numbers: a woman I coached who was preparing for pregnancy told me this smoothie was the first "dessert" in years that didn't come with a morning-after of guilt and hunger, and that having it in her toolkit changed how she felt about her evenings more than any rule she'd ever tried. That's what a good swap does. It doesn't restrict. It makes the better thing the easier thing.

A few more swaps for specific cravings, since they come up. Salty and crunchy: roasted chickpeas, seaweed snacks, olives, nuts with a little salt. Creamy: the yogurt bowl, avocado on anything, a spoon of nut butter. Chocolate: the smoothie, or a square of eighty-five percent with almonds, eaten with the mindful first bite. Bread and pasta: not banned, but paired, a smaller portion with a big protein and vegetable share, and the walk after. And the craving for a glass of wine at the end of the day, which is often a craving for the ritual of stopping: the berry-basil sparkling water in a real glass, the lights dimmed, the same chair. Keep the ritual; change what's in the glass.

— 15:30–18:30  THE COUPLES ANGLE: CRAVING DATES —

Now the couples angle, which I think is the most underrated tool in this whole session. A craving date is a non-food treat you plan together, in advance, for the craving hour. It works on two roots at once: the emotional root, because you're getting connection instead of sugar, and the environmental root, because you're somewhere the cue isn't.

Ideas. The after-dinner walk with a thermos of the tea. A board game or a puzzle at the table where the snacks used to be. A bath with two mugs, one at a time while the other reads aloud. A drive to see the sunset. The warm-touch exercise from Module Six, ten minutes, phones away. An evening at the pottery studio, the climbing wall, the library, anywhere with hands busy and no dessert menu. And the simplest: getting into bed at nine with a book, together, which is a craving date and a sleep habit at the same time.

The rule is that you plan it on Sunday, for the two or three evenings that are your hardest, and you treat it as a date, not a diet tactic. Nobody says the word "craving." You're just two people doing something nice on a Tuesday. Solo: the same list, with a friend on the phone, or with yourself and a real intention.

And a word on the rest of the evening, because the craving date only covers part of it. After the date, the sleep routine from Module Four takes over: screens off, the warm shower, the gratitude at the pillow. Most late-night cravings arrive in the gap between the end of the evening's activity and the beginning of sleep, the hour of scrolling. Close that gap, by going to bed earlier than you think you need to, and the craving has nowhere to live. In my own house, the single change that quieted the ten p.m. craving most was not a swap. It was a bedtime.

— 18:30–19:30  SUSTAINABILITY AND TRACKING —

Tracking, lightly. The workbook has a page: date, time, the root you think it was, the tool you used, and whether the wave passed. That's four columns. If you prefer an app, a simple habit tracker or a notes app works; the point is to see, after two weeks, which two tools are yours, because everyone ends up with two. Then the toolkit shrinks to something you can carry in your head.

— 19:30–20:00  ACTION HANDOFF —

Make the fix smoothie this week and upload a photo, then plan one craving date and talk it through with your partner, or your person, for ten XP. Session Three is about freedom: keeping this for the long haul, and your questions, answered.

lessons.title: Session 3: Long-Term Craving Freedom
lessons.description: Habit audits, relapse plan, fertility impact, Q&A.
lessons.transcript:
THE FIX FOR CRAVINGS — SESSION 3: LONG-TERM CRAVING FREEDOM — 20 MIN

— 0:00–0:30  HOOK —

The hardest part of changing a craving isn't the first week. It's month four, when the novelty is gone, the tools feel ordinary, and something in life goes sideways. That's when most people slide, and that's when the people who've built what I call craving freedom don't. The difference is not strength. It's a plan for month four, written in month one. This session is that plan.

— 0:30–6:30  MAINTENANCE: AUDITS AND RELAPSE PLANS —

Maintenance has two tools. The first is the habit audit, and it ties straight to Module Seven. Once a month, three questions. Which tools am I still using? Which cues have crept back: the drawer refilled, the show and the snack reunited, the coffee moved to three p.m.? And what changed in my life that changed my cravings: sleep, stress, a season, a relationship? Cravings are signals, and a rising craving in month four is usually reporting a change somewhere else. The audit reads the report. The workbook has the three questions on a single page you fill in on the first of the month.

The second tool is the relapse plan, and I want to teach the science properly, because it's some of the most useful in addiction psychology. Alan Marlatt studied why people who had changed a behavior returned to it, and found the pattern was almost never a single slip. It was what happened after: the abstinence violation effect, in which one lapse triggers a story, "I've blown it, I'm back where I started, I might as well," and the story does the damage the lapse didn't. Polivy and Herman found the same in dieters, the what-the-hell effect. And Adams and Leary showed the antidote in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology: people guided to respond to a lapse with self-compassion ate less afterward than those who weren't.

So the relapse plan has four parts, and it's written before you need it. One: the high-risk situations. Be specific. "The week before my period." "Travel." "The night after a negative test." "Mother visiting." Two: the early warning signs. "I start buying 'for guests.'" "I skip the walk twice." "Bedtime drifts past eleven." Three: the slip script, the exact sentence you'll say after eating the thing: "That was a slip, not a fall. I'm going to drink a glass of water and do the next thing on my plan." Four: the reset, the three tiny actions you'll take in the next twenty-four hours, and the person you'll text the word "reset" to. The workbook has this as a one-page template, and completing it is your action for this session.

One more piece of Marlatt's work that I find freeing: he found that people who expected occasional lapses and planned for them did better than people who aimed for perfection. Perfection is a relapse risk. A plan for imperfection is protection.

Let me walk you through a relapse plan filled in, so you can see the shape. High-risk situations: the week before my period; my mother-in-law's visits, which come with a full biscuit tin; the night after a scan. Early warning signs: I start keeping "a little something" in the car; I skip the after-dinner walk two nights running; I'm in bed with my phone at eleven. Slip script: "That was a slip, not a fall. Water, then the walk tomorrow." Reset: text my sister the word "reset"; protein-first breakfast tomorrow; the ten-minute pause at the first craving; bed by ten. That plan fits on an index card, and the index card lives in the kitchen drawer where the biscuits used to be.

— 6:30–11:30  FERTILITY IMPACT: STABLE BLOOD SUGAR, HORMONE HARMONY —

Let me close the loop on why craving freedom is a fertility practice, with the research laid out plainly. In the Nurses' Health Study, Jorge Chavarro's team found that women whose diets carried a higher glycemic load, more fast-digesting carbohydrate, had a higher risk of ovulatory infertility, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. In a large Australian and international cohort of first pregnancies, published in Human Reproduction, women who ate fast food four or more times a week before conception took longer to become pregnant and had a higher risk of infertility than women who rarely did, while those who ate fruit three or more times a day conceived faster. In women with PCOS, a low-glycemic diet improved insulin sensitivity and menstrual regularity in a trial in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. For men, the Salas-Huetos review found sugar-sweetened drinks and processed food associated with poorer semen quality. And across nearly four thousand couples in the study in Epidemiology, a daily sugary drink meant about twenty percent lower odds of conceiving each month, for both partners.

The thread is insulin. Stable blood sugar means stable insulin; stable insulin means the ovaries aren't being pushed toward extra androgens and the whole hormonal conversation between brain, ovary, and testis runs with less noise. That's what "hormone harmony" means when I use the phrase: not a mystical balance, a signaling system with less static. Every craving you ride out, every swap with protein and fat, every early night, is a little less static. That's the fertility impact of THE FIX, and it's measurable in the research.

And one more, because it's about the kind of freedom I mean. A body that isn't riding a blood-sugar rollercoaster has steadier energy, steadier mood, and steadier patience, and those are the qualities the rest of this journey, the waiting, the appointments, the conversations, will ask of you most. Freedom from cravings is liberation. It's fuel for the miracle ahead.

There's a longer horizon to this too, and it's the reason THE FIX sits inside a course about family. The relationship with food that you build now is the one a child will watch. The parent who can have one square of chocolate with attention, who doesn't eat in secret, who doesn't moralize about "good" and "bad" food, who goes for a walk when the day was hard, is teaching all of that without a word. Craving freedom is not only yours. It's one of the first things your family will inherit, through the marks on the cells being built this month and through the ordinary example of a Tuesday evening.

— 11:30–17:30  Q&A: YOUR QUESTIONS —

Now your questions, from the forum.

"How do I handle cravings when I'm traveling?" Travel breaks every cue and every routine, so plan the environment before you go. Pack the swaps: walnuts, dark chocolate, a protein bar with a short ingredient list, tea bags. Eat protein at breakfast wherever you are; hotel eggs are your friend. Walk on arrival. And lower the bar: on the road, the goal is no sweet alone and one honest night's sleep, not the full plan.

"What about the days before my period?" Cravings rise, energy falls, and it's hormones, not weakness. Add protein and fat to every meal that week, expect the wave to be bigger, use the pause and the fix smoothie more often, and don't audit yourself on those days. Write it in the tracker so you can see the pattern next month and plan for it.

"My partner keeps bringing sweets home. What do I do?" Module Six, not Module Two. An "I" statement: "I feel scared when the sweets are on the counter, because I'm working so hard, and I'd like them kept out of sight." Ask for one thing, not for them to change their eating. And the craving date is your friend here; it gives you both something to do on the hard evenings that isn't a negotiation about the pantry.

"Are artificial sweeteners a good swap?" Not the way people hope. The research is mixed, but intensely sweet tastes keep the sweet expectation alive and give you none of the protein, fat, and fiber that quiets the loop. A diet soda occasionally is not a crisis; six a day is the old groove in a new costume. The better swap is the berry-basil sparkling water.

"Does it get easier?" Yes, and I'll tell you how it gets easier, because it isn't the way people expect. The cravings don't vanish. They get quieter and rarer, and, more importantly, they stop meaning anything. A craving at month six is a passing thought, not a crisis, because you've ridden a hundred of them and you know what's on the other side. That's what freedom feels like: not the absence of the wave, but the certainty that you can surf it.

"What do I do about the guilt from the years before?" The body clears. The cells being built now are built from now. The insulin environment of the next three months starts today, whatever the last ten years held. You're not making up for the past; you're preparing the future, and only one of those is your job. Set the guilt down. It doesn't get a seat at the table, and it never helped you eat one vegetable.

"How do I explain this to friends who think I'm being extreme?" You don't have to explain, and if you do, keep it short and about you: "I've learned that sugar was running my evenings and I'm changing that." Not a lecture, not a conversion. The people who love you will notice you have more energy and ask. The ones who tease are usually negotiating with their own drawer. And at a party, the fix is simple: eat protein before you go, hold a sparkling water, and enjoy the one thing you actually want with the mindful first bite.

"I slipped badly last week. Have I undone everything?" No. Lally's research: a missed day doesn't matter. The body clears: a week of sugar doesn't undo three months of steadier insulin, and the next three months start today. Say the slip script, do the reset, and text your person. You didn't fall. You slipped, and you're already back on the path, because you're here asking.

— 17:30–19:30  WRAP AND HEART-LED CLOSE —

Here's what the long view looks like. The number of cravings that win drifts down over the first two months, and then it stops dropping and settles somewhere low. That settling is the freedom. From there, your job is the monthly audit, the relapse plan in the drawer, the two tools you've kept, and grace on the weeks that wobble. That's all. You don't have to fight this forever. You have to know what to do when it shows up, and now you do.

As someone who lived inside cravings for years and built a life outside them, I want to leave you with the sentence I wish someone had said to me at the start: you are not weak, you were wired, and wiring can be rewired. You've just done it, in three sessions and a few weeks of practice. Fuel your body for the miracle ahead, and let this freedom be one of the first things your family inherits from you.

— 19:30–20:00  ACTION HANDOFF —

Complete the relapse plan template in the Cravings Fix Workbook and upload it, then share your fix success in the forum, however small, for ten XP. And listen to the session-summaries audio whenever you need the three sessions in four minutes. Thank you for doing this work with me.

— SESSION SUMMARIES AUDIO (SCRIPT) —

THE FIX FOR CRAVINGS — SESSION SUMMARIES AUDIO — 4 MIN

— 0:00–0:20  INTRO —

Hello, it's Cynthia. This is THE FIX for Cravings in four minutes: the three sessions, summarized, for the moment a craving is standing in the room and you need the whole thing fast.

— 0:20–1:30  SESSION ONE IN ONE MINUTE —

A craving has two roots. An emotional root, in the wanting circuit that learned sugar means relief. And a physical root, in the blood-sugar swing the last sugar set up hours ago. Both are real; both can be rewired, because the same brain that built the groove can build a new one, with repetition. Five strategies: the pause, "there it is," a timer, hands busy, ride the wave. The swap, sweet with protein and fat, never sweet alone, and fix the meal before your craving hour. The cue, rearranged, so the drawer and the show and the drive stop firing. Sleep, because tonight's craving was scheduled by this morning's alarm. And the emotional root: what do I actually need right now, and give yourself the real thing.

— 1:30–2:40  SESSION TWO IN ONE MINUTE —

Six tools, in order: pause, sip something warm, move for five minutes, swap, connect with one text, and sleep earlier. Match the tool to the root: physical, swap and move; environmental, rearrange and sip; emotional, pause and connect and the honest question. The fix smoothie: Greek yogurt, cocoa, nut butter, half a frozen banana, spinach, cinnamon, a pinch of salt. Or the two-minute bowl: yogurt, cocoa, nut butter, frozen cherries. And the craving date: a non-food treat you plan on Sunday for your hardest evenings, with your partner or your person, where nobody says the word craving.

— 2:40–3:40  SESSION THREE IN ONE MINUTE —

Maintenance is a monthly audit, three questions: which tools am I still using, which cues crept back, what changed in my life. And a relapse plan, written before you need it: the high-risk situations, the early warning signs, the slip script, "that was a slip, not a fall," and the reset, three tiny actions and one text. Perfection is a relapse risk; a plan for imperfection is protection. Stable blood sugar means stable insulin means clearer hormone signaling; that's the fertility impact, and it's in the research.

— 3:40–4:00  CLOSE —

You are not weak. You were wired, and wiring can be rewired. Ride the wave. Text your person. Go to bed. I'm proud of you.

lessons.description: Live Q&A recap, group shares, three quick wins.
lessons.notes: All Replays nav; edit for clarity.
lessons.transcript:
REPLAY 1: GROUP COACHING — NUTRITION AND CRAVINGS DEEP DIVE — 35 MIN (LIVE-CALL FACILITATION SCRIPT)

— 0:00–5:00  INTRO AND RECAP —

Welcome, everyone. I can see the room filling up, and I want to start by saying what I say at the top of every live call: this community is your support net. Nothing you ask here is too small, too strange, or too much. Lean in; it's for your conception dreams, and it's for each other.

Let's recap where we are, for anyone who joined recently. Module One taught us that cravings are signals, not weaknesses: they have three roots, emotional, environmental, physiological, and tracking them for three days is one of the most powerful things you can do. Module Two gave us the fertility plate, the sugar swaps that actually satisfy, hydration, gut health, meal planning, the celiac-test-before-gluten-free rule, supplements with your doctor in the loop, and the seven-day challenge. And THE FIX, for those who've watched the bonuses, went deeper into rewiring.

Before questions, a quick check-in poll in the chat: type one word for how your afternoons feel this week compared with when you started. I'll read a few.

— 5:00–25:00  Q&A HIGHLIGHTS (PREPARED ANSWERS; LIVE QUESTIONS INTERLEAVE) —

Question: "How do I handle cravings when I'm traveling?" Here's what I tell everyone. Travel removes every cue and routine at once, so build the environment before you leave. Pack the swaps, walnuts, dark chocolate, tea bags, a short-ingredient protein bar. Protein at breakfast wherever you are; hotel eggs are your friend. Walk on arrival; it resets sleep and blood sugar together. And lower the bar: on the road, the goal is no sweet alone and one honest night's sleep. A study in Nutrition Reviews on real-world eating patterns made a point I've found true in every kitchen and every airport: the people who keep healthy habits aren't the ones with the most willpower, they're the ones whose environment does most of the work. Pack your environment.

Question: "I have PCOS. Does the fertility plate change for me?" It sharpens. The Endocrine Society's guideline puts lifestyle first for PCOS, and the research on low-glycemic eating in PCOS, the trial in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found improved insulin sensitivity and more regular cycles. So for you: the slow-carb quarter of the plate stays small and slow, beans and oats rather than white rice; protein and fat at every meal without exception; the after-meal walk from Module Three, which is the single best PCOS habit I know; and ask your doctor about myo-inositol, which we covered in the supplements training. Your plan runs alongside your specialist, not instead.

Question: "My partner won't change how he eats. What can I actually do?" Two things, and neither is nagging. First, biology, once, gently: half of fertility rests with him, his sperm is rebuilt every three months from what he eats, sleeps, and drinks, and the walnut study is two handfuls a day with nothing removed. Many men have simply never been told. Second, cook the plate and put it on the table without a lecture; a beautiful dinner persuades better than a study. And keep your own column full. The JAMA Internal Medicine research says your changes make his more likely, whether or not he's decided yet.

Question: "Is coffee okay?" Moderate coffee, one to two cups, hasn't been linked to reduced fertility in the ASRM's review, and ACOG's ceiling in pregnancy is two hundred milligrams a day. So: find your ceiling now and stay under it, keep it to the morning so it doesn't steal your sleep, and follow each cup with a glass of water. Energy drinks, no.

Question: "What about the evenings? That's when I fall apart." The evening craving is almost always scheduled earlier: a low-protein lunch, a short night, or an unprocessed day. So the fix is at noon and at bedtime, not at nine p.m. Protein and fat at lunch. The after-dinner walk. Phone to the kitchen at nine. And for the moment itself, the pause, "there it is," a timer, the tea, and the fix bowl if you're still hungry after ten minutes. If the evenings are about the hard day rather than the blood sugar, that's Module Four's question: what do I actually need? Usually it's rest.

Question: "I keep hearing about gut health. Where do I even start?" One tablespoon of sauerkraut or a quarter cup of kefir, once a day, for two weeks, then build. Aim for thirty different plants a week, counting herbs and spices. Fiber up slowly with plenty of water. The Stanford study in Cell saw diversity rise and inflammation fall within ten weeks of daily fermented foods. Don't start with a probiotic supplement; start with food, and ask your doctor or a dietitian about supplements if you're considering one.

Question: "Sweeteners: yes or no?" Mostly no, not because they're poison but because they keep the sweet expectation alive and give you none of the protein and fat that quiets the loop. Berry-basil sparkling water is the swap. An occasional diet soda is not a crisis.

Question: "I did the elimination and I feel better without gluten. Do I still need the test?" Yes, and please hear the order: the celiac blood test only works while you're eating gluten, so if you've been off it for weeks, talk to your doctor about a supervised gluten challenge before testing. Knowing whether it's celiac disease changes your care for life and matters for absorption of the nutrients a pregnancy needs. Feeling better is information; the test is the answer.

— 25:00–30:00  ACTIONABLE TAKEAWAYS: THREE QUICK WINS —

Let me pull three quick wins out of everything we've said, so you leave with something for tonight.

One: fix the meal before your craving hour. If it's three p.m., it's lunch; if it's nine p.m., it's dinner and the walk. Protein and fat, every time.

Two: put one fermented food on the counter where you'll see it: sauerkraut, kefir, plain yogurt. One spoon a day. That's the gut training in one habit.

Three: the pause. "There it is," ten-minute timer, something warm in your hands. Ride the wave. Most of them are shorter than the kettle.

And for partners, one more: two handfuls of walnuts a day. Nothing removed.

— 30:00–35:00  CLOSING —

Thank you for showing up tonight, for the questions and for the honesty. I'll update the Cravings FAQ with anything new that came up, and it'll be in the resources under this replay. If you're watching this as a recording: mark it complete for ten XP, and then take one insight or one question to the forum for twenty, because the question you didn't ask tonight is the one someone else needs answered.

This community is your support net. Lean in for your conception dreams, and I'll see you on the next call.

lessons.title: Emotional Wellness and Connection
lessons.description: Fertility emotions, partner conflict, role-plays, homework.
lessons.transcript:
REPLAY 2: GROUP COACHING — EMOTIONAL WELLNESS AND CONNECTION — 40 MIN (LIVE-CALL FACILITATION SCRIPT)

— 0:00–5:00  THEME INTRO AND CHECK-IN POLL —

Welcome back, everyone. Tonight is the heart call. We're going to talk about the emotions of this journey, frustration, envy, grief, hope, all of them, and about what happens between two people when those emotions arrive at different times and in different shapes. These replays are here to remind you that you're not alone on this heart-led path, and tonight especially I'd like you to feel that.

Let's start with a check-in poll. Look at the emotion wheel from Module Four, and type the one word that's closest to where you are tonight. Not "fine." The real word.

Before we go on, the support slide. If anything tonight brings up more than you can hold, the resources are on screen: your doctor, your clinic's counselor, the crisis line for your country, and the organizations in the Emotion Wheel PDF. Reaching out is one of the tools.

— 5:00–30:00  KEY DISCUSSIONS —

Theme: "We grieve differently, and it's tearing us apart." Let me draw something on the whiteboard.

Here's what the research on couples facing infertility keeps finding, and it's summarized in the European fertility society's guideline on psychosocial care: partners tend to cope differently, and each reads the other's style as not caring. One wants to talk for an hour; the other wants to go for a run. Neither is wrong, and the run is not indifference; it's a nervous system regulating itself the only way it knows. The fix is the sentence from Module Four: "When I'm upset I need you to listen, not fix." "When I go quiet, I'm processing; ask me in an hour." Say it now, out loud, on a good day, so it's already said on the bad one.

Theme: "The negative test." I want to say the thing from Module Four again, because people need to hear it in a room, not just in a video. Jacky Boivin's meta-analysis in the BMJ found that women's distress before treatment was not associated with whether the treatment worked. Your anxiety did not cause the negative test. And the ESHRE guideline says that distress on this journey is common enough that clinics should screen for it and refer. So: the coping plan, written calm. Emotion, trigger, body, first tool, second tool, who you'll tell, what you'll say to yourself, and a boundary. Let's build one together on the whiteboard for the negative test.

Theme: "The fight about habits." Somebody always asks this, because this course starts it. One of you cleared the pantry; the other came home to no chocolate. This is Module Six: soft start-up, "I" statement, the listening loop, a timeout if either of you is flooded, a repair attempt, one small agreement, and a gratitude to close. I'll draw the flowchart.

Gottman's research: the first three minutes predict the ending; contempt is the strongest predictor of trouble; a twenty-minute break and a return beats pushing on; five positives to one negative. The habit fight resolved well is a rehearsal for every fight you'll have as parents.

Theme: "Extended family and the questions." "When are you two going to…" Boundaries are preparation, not rudeness. A script: "We're not discussing timelines, but we'd love your help with Sunday dinner." Leave the baby shower early. Mute the account. Protecting your nervous system in this window is part of the plan.

Theme: "I'm doing this alone." Then you've done something harder than most, and this room is your circle. The connection practices are the same with a friend, a sibling, a parent, or the person you met in the forum. Say who your person is in the chat tonight, and if you don't have one yet, say that, and watch what happens.

— 30:00–35:00  BREAKTHROUGHS AND INTEGRATION —

Let me integrate, because tonight's two themes are one theme. Stress hormones dampen the brain's signals to the ovaries and testes; that's the Module Four science. Connection, being listened to, touched kindly, on the same team, raises oxytocin and lowers those stress markers; that's Module Six. So a couple that can name a feeling, listen for four minutes, repair a fight, and share a gratitude at the pillow is building the hormone environment as surely as a couple eating the fertility plate. The heart work is body work. It always was.

— 35:00–40:00  HOMEWORK AND CLOSING —

Homework, and it's small. One ten-minute listening session this week, four minutes each way, with the prompt "something about this journey I haven't said." One coping plan, written calm, for the situation you fear most. And one gratitude, tonight, at the pillow, to your partner or to yourself.

If you're watching the recording: mark it complete and reflect for ten XP, then apply one tip, the listening session is the one I'd choose, and post what happened in the forum for ten. The Connection Q&A Notes under this replay have every tool we drew tonight, and the full transcript will be there once it's edited.

These replays remind you that you're not alone on this heart-led path. Thank you for being here, for the words you typed at the start, and for the ones you're going to say to each other tonight. I'll see you in the forum.

For the last month: 0 = never · 1 = sometimes · 2 = often · 3 = most days

Not a diagnosis. See your doctor promptly for: blood in stool, unexplained weight loss, severe or persistent pain, symptoms that are worsening, or a family history of bowel disease or celiac disease.

Antibiotic courses in the last year (0 = none, 1 = one, 2 = two, 3 = three+)

quizzes.title: Baby Steps Pre-Course Survey
quizzes.intro: Before we begin, take five unhurried minutes to answer these four questions. There are no wrong answers. Your responses are private to Cynthia and the support team, and you will come back to them in Module 7 to see how far you have travelled.

questions.text: What is your BIG WHY for this conception journey? Write it the way you would say it to someone you trust.

What will you DO, BE and CHANGE to accomplish them? (one line for each if it helps)
Is there anything you would like Cynthia to know before you start? (optional: health context, past attempts, worries)
Are you completing the course with a partner?
